title.narrative: UNDP- Att stärka motståndskraften hos hushållen i Guatemalas torra korridor
UNDP- Strengthening the resilience of households in Guatemala's dry corridor

description.narrative:
Programmet syftar till att förbättra tillgången till säker och näringsriktig mat för familjer och samhällen i den så kallade "torra korridoren" i Jalapa och Chiquimula i Guatemala. Detta kommer ske genom förbättrad och hållbar användning av naturresurser (skog, mark), integrerad vattenförvaltning (Integrated Water Resource Management), samt genom att stärka motståndskraft och anpassning till klimatförändringar. Programmet avser främja god samhällsstyrning samt jämställdhet mellan könen. Säkrad tillgång till vatten ligger i fokus med särskild tonvikt på kvinnor och barn. De urfolk som bor i regionen inkluderar Ch´ortí´ i Chiquimula och Pocomán i Jalapa. FAO samordnar arbetet och även UNICEF, UNDP och WHO deltar. Den torra korridoren är ett landområde Guatemala med låg nederbörd och näringsfattig mark där utkomsten av jordbruket är lågt.
Förväntade resultat av programmet inkluderar:
1. Förbättrade och jämlika system på lokal nivå för säkrad tillgång till näringsriktiga livsmedel, främjande av biologisk mångfald, och ökad motståndskraft och anpassning till klimatförändringar. Detta ska uppnås genom ökad kunskap kring hållbara metoder inom jordbruket och hållbart nyttjande av naturresurser.
2. Familjer och lokala organisationer stärkta i sin kapacitet att utkräva sin rättigheter, samtidigt som lokala myndigheter ska ha ökat sin kapacitet att effektivt utföra sitt arbete och möjliggöra åtnjutande av rättigheter. Myndigheter och lokala organisationer ska gemensamt kunna identifiera behov kring vatten- och markförvaltning och infrastruktur i arbetet med lokala planer för utveckling. Dessa ska ta hänsyn till åtgärder för att öka motståndskraft till naturkatastrofer genom riskreducerande åtgärder. Utvecklingsplanerna kommer också inkludera hälsovård, förbättrad produktion av och tillgång till livsmedel. Arbetet ska genomsyras av ett aktivt arbete för att främja jämställdhet och öka kvinnors deltagande i beslutsprocesser.
3. Stärkt kapacitet hos lokala myndigheter att effektivt implementera social politik och garantera människors åtnjutande av rättigheter och möta identifierade behov. Dialogen med rättsinnehavare ska ha stärkts kring framtagande av investeringsförslag till utvecklingsråden kring livsmedelssäkerhet och hållbart nyttjande av naturresurser och riskreducering.

The program aims to improve food and nutritional security for families and communities in 7 micro-watersheds of Jalapa and Chiquimula in the Dry Corridor of Guatemala, through the improvement of sustainable use of natural resources (forest, soil), integrated water management and increased resilience capacities for climate change adaptation. The implementation includes promoting and improving governance, gender equality and water security with special emphasis in women and children. The indigenous groups in the area are Ch´ortí´ in Chiquimula and Pocomán in Jalapa. FAO will be the lead agency, working in coordination in field with UNICEF, UNDP and WHO. The Dry corridor is a portion of land in Guatemala affected by reduced precipitation, weak soil and low yields located at the rural area. The program.
At the end of the intervention the joint program is expected to:
1. Improve communitarian food systems, food and nutritional security, biodiversity, resilience and climate change adaptation through strengthened knowledge in agriculture good practices, nutrition, sustainable use and management of natural resources and the promotion of gender equality. 2. Families, community organizations strengthened as right holders and Municipalities with improved capacities as public servants and duty bearers to jointly identify needs to plan gray and green water infrastructure for water management, health, land use planning, municipal development plans and disaster risk prevention to improve food availability/production, food security, resilience, climate change adaptation and women participation and decision making. 3. Strengthened capacities at ministries and municipal officials, members of the development councils, food security and nutrition commissions and National Coordinator for risk disaster prevention - CONRED coordinators, to perform their legal responsibilities as duty bearers, activate public policy in territories and improve dialogue with right holders to design and present investment proposals for development councils for food security and nutrition, water security, climate change adaptation and resilience.

sector.narrative: Multisector aid for basic social services

title.narrative: Program Document Dry Corridor Joint Program

description.narrative:
The Joint Program applies a human rights based approach which seeks the empowerment of rights holders and their protection through strengthened institutional capacities and sustainable community-based strategies.
During 2024, the program continued its work along key lines of action; a) development of climate-adapted and drought-resilient food systems, b) strengthening of knowledge, attitudes, and practices for improved nutrition and health, c) improved water and sanitation governance, and d) enhanced municipal and community capacities for planning, coordination, and risk management.
A total of 7 municipalities and over 57 communities in Chiquimula and Jalapa benefited directly from the program. Special emphasis was placed on the participation of women (over 50% of beneficiaries) and Indigenous peoples, particularly Chorti communities, in order to strengthen resilience, food security, and equality.
Examples of results achieved during the period from January 2024 to December 2024:
Food production and food security: - 1,191 families increased their maize yields by 20.99% and beans by 15.89% compared to the baseline.
- 28 communities implemented agricultural and livestock ventures, which generated sustainable economic income. Furthermore, 227 community promoters were trained in soil management and conservation practices, the use of drought-resistant varieties, and water management in livestock production.
- Families reported an average 12% increase in monthly household income, from $110.30 in the baseline to U$123.50 during the year 2024.
Coffee production and value chains:
- 109 small-scale coffee producers (47% women, 20% youth) have a cultivated area of 148 hectares, of which 113 hectares are implementing the sustainable profitability model, producing 43 metric tons of certified coffee.
- 80% of farms were certified under Rainforest Alliance and Coffee Practices standards, enabling access to premium markets.
- Four bio-factories were installed, producing a total of 3,200 liters of bio-inputs, reducing costs and strengthening agroecological practices.
- 20 youth and women were trained in coffee quality and cupping, expanding their role in specialized coffee value chains.
Community governance:
- 117 municipal officials and 38 community leaders were trained in risk management with a gender perspective, strengthening local planning and governance structures.
Agents of Change:
- Women, mostly Indigenous Ch'orti', trained as Agents of Change, replicating practices in health, hygiene and nutrition across rural communities.
Health and housing:
- Through Vivienda Saludable and Mano a Mano initiatives, households accessed dignified housing solutions linked to better sanitation and family health.
Relevant Results Achieved
- Target groups that previously produced mainly for substance are now capable of producing surplus grains and marketing certified coffee, thereby diversifying both diets and income.
- Women and youth have gained new economic roles in production, processing, and marketing - groups that were underrepresented in earlier stages.
- Certified coffee production has linked local producers to differentiated and premium markets, strengthening resilience against price fluctuations.
- The program demonstrates that Indigenous Ch'orti' communities can successfully apply climate-adapted and sustainable practices to increase yields and income.
- Local water and sanitation offices (OMAS) enhanced their technical capacity for community monitoring and awareness.
Lessons Learned
- Combining technical assistance with local leadership (community promoters, youth and women coffee leaders) accelerates adoption of new practices and ensures continuity.
- Certification schemes not only raise incomes but also increase women's and youth's participation in decision-making processes, challenging traditional gender roles.
- The establishment of bio-factories has proved cost-effective and strengthened local autonomy in input production, showing potential for scaling.
- Linking agricultural interventions with climate forecasts and early warning systems has improved families' adaptive capacity to drought.
Delays
In contrast to 2023, the 2024 implementation did not report major delays. Activities were generally carried out as planned under the adjusted work plan.
Implementation was delayed in some municipalities due to changes in government personnel, requiring preliminary activities to reintroduce the program and validate prior agreements. The situation stabilized over the year and did not significantly impact planned outcomes.
Challenges
Persistent challenges remain in:
- Ensuring sustainability and institutionalization of strategies such as Healthy Municipalities and Healthy Housing.
- Limited municipal technical capacity in water and sanitation service management, which constrains scaling-up.
- External risks such as heavy rainfall and market fluctuations (for example coffee prices) which continue to affect family livelihoods.
- Migration patterns, as many households rely on temporary migration for income, which can disrupt continuity of community-based processes.
